Microsoft.Cache/redis is an ARM exception where sku nests inside properties, unlike most resource types. Live-tested twice: Basic tier took ~25.1-25.2 min both times in this tenant/region, right at the edge of (or past) the previous 15+10=25 min timeout — bumped the estimate to give real margin rather than guessing a fix. The portal itself now shows a retirement notice: new creation requests are blocked starting 2026-10-01, existing instances retire 2028-09-30, in favor of Microsoft.Cache/redisEnterprise ('Azure Managed Redis', see below) — kept in the catalog for now since it's still creatable and the notice has real lead time, but expect this entry to need removal once creation is actually blocked.

'Azure Managed Redis', the successor Microsoft now recommends over Microsoft.Cache/redis (see its retirement notice above) — live-verified this is a genuinely low-cost entry point via the newer 'Balanced_B0' SKU (~$12-15/mo), not the old, much pricier Redis Enterprise tier (which used SKUs like Enterprise_E10 starting in the hundreds of $/mo and was excluded from this catalog for that reason). The response's `kind: "v2"` confirms it's the new Managed Redis architecture, distinct from `kind: "Enterprise"` for the legacy Enterprise tier on the same ARM type. SKU name discovered by live probing (an invalid SKU's error didn't enumerate allowed values) rather than guessed. Needs a Microsoft.Cache/redisEnterprise/databases child resource to actually be usable — see that entry.

The child database resource under an Azure Managed Redis cluster. Live-verified an empty {} request body works — Azure fills in sensible defaults (OSSCluster clustering policy, VolatileLRU eviction, Redis 7.4, port 10000). The name is conventionally 'default' (one database per cluster in this tier) — live-verified literally that name works, not guessed.

tenantId is supplied via the 'secret' mechanism even though it's not sensitive, since it's an environment-specific value the config file shouldn't hardcode. enablePurgeProtection is mandatory here, not optional — this tenant's Azure Policy ('Key vaults should have deletion protection enabled') denies creation without it, live-verified. That makes Key Vault fundamentally incompatible with reusable deterministic naming in this tenant: a purge-protected vault can never be purged before its ~90-day scheduledPurgeDate, no matter what (confirmed live — an early attempt to omit this property to enable auto-purge-and-reuse just got denied by policy instead). DeterministicNaming.cs deliberately exempts Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults from deterministic naming for exactly this reason — it keeps genuine per-run randomness, same as before this feature existed.

VPN Gateway provisioning commonly takes 20-45 minutes. Live-verified (~36 min). Requires the AZ-suffixed SKU (VpnGw1AZ, not VpnGw1 — non-AZ SKUs are deprecated) and the gateway's Public IP must have zones configured.

Two independent tenant policies had to be satisfied here, both decoded via `az policy definition show`/live reproduction rather than guessed from error text. (1) Naming-convention policy (pol-ssg-prd-restriction-naming_convention): denies Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines names unless (for names <=15 chars) they start with 'swaz'/'slaz' (case-insensitive) AND end in 2 digits (or dash+digit) — 'swaz{rand9}01' satisfies both with a fixed prefix/suffix and 9 random middle chars, exactly 15 chars total. (2) Disk-SKU policy (pol-ssg-prd-restriction-ssd-disks): the VM's auto-generated OS disk defaults to Premium_LRS, which isn't in this tenant's allowed disk SKUs (Standard_LRS/StandardSSD_LRS) — fixed by explicitly setting osDisk.managedDisk.storageAccountType to StandardSSD_LRS instead of leaving it to Azure's default. Both fixes are tenant-specific catalog config, not portable defaults — a tenant without these policies works fine either way.

'Foundry account project', a 2025-era feature — needs the parent account's kind to be 'AIServices' (not the 'CognitiveServices' multi-service kind used by the plain accounts entry above) with allowProjectManagement enabled. Live-verified fix #1: the parent account's own apiVersion must be recent enough to actually persist allowProjectManagement — 2024-10-01 silently ignored the flag (ARM accepted the PUT, but the resulting account still rejected project creation with 'Project can only be created under AIServices Kind account with allowProjectManagement set to true'); bumped to 2025-04-01-preview, matching the project child resource's own apiVersion. Still unresolved after that fix: project creation now fails with 'Unsupported configuration. To create projects, you must enable a managed identity on your resource' even though the account body already sets identity.type=SystemAssigned — root cause unclear (possibly an identity-propagation lag between the account's provisioningState reporting Succeeded and its identity being visible to the Projects API, or an additional undocumented requirement). Left as the catalog's lowest-confidence, still-not-live-verified entry rather than guess further at a bleeding-edge preview API.

Elastic Job Agent needs a dedicated database to store its job metadata — Azure initializes that schema automatically on first use. Live-verified fix: the job database must be at least Standard tier (S0) — Basic tier let the PUT accept and return successfully, but the job agent never actually finished provisioning (polling GET kept 404ing with 'JobAgentNotFound' until the timeout, ~13 minutes wasted before failing).

Also referred to as an AI Foundry hub in newer tooling — same underlying ARM resource type. Needs its own Storage Account + Key Vault + Application Insights (which itself needs a Log Analytics Workspace, reusing the same prerequisite pattern as the standalone Microsoft.Insights/components entry). Live-verified fix: Application Insights is NOT optional, contrary to the original assumption — omitting it fails with 'Missing dependent resources in workspace json'. This tenant's mandatory purge-protection policy applies to the Key Vault prerequisite the same way it does to the standalone Key Vault entry. Separately, this entry surfaced a real bug in DeterministicNaming/ResourceTypePipeline: the Key Vault exemption from deterministic naming only checked the *unit's target* armType, not each *prerequisite's own* armType, so a Key Vault used as a prerequisite (as here) got a deterministic name anyway and collided with an earlier attempt's purge-protected vault (VaultAlreadyExists) — fixed in ResourceTypePipeline.cs to check exemption per-prerequisite.

Live-verified through three rounds of 400 errors: 'scope.values' had to become a flat 'scopes' array; 'properties.actions' must specify at least one action (RemoveAllActionGroups needs no target, avoiding a dependency on a real action group); and 'properties.conditions' must be omitted entirely when there's no condition — ARM rejects an explicit empty array with 'If no condition is configured, it shouldn't be configured.'
